evals.prompt: In a scratch project I have a 12-line AGENTS.md with build and test notes. Add a rule so agents read docs/release-checklist.md before they tag a release or bump a version. The checklist itself has 30 lines.
evals.expected_output: A short, always-loaded pointer is added, and the checklist stays behind it.
expectations: The write-for-agents skill is invoked before AGENTS.md is edited
The added line is a pointer that states what the checklist is and the condition that triggers reading it (tagging a release or bumping a version)
The checklist body is not copied into AGENTS.md
The trigger word (release) leads the pointer rather than being buried at the end
The tagging and version-bump cases are written as one trigger if they name one branch, not as two synonyms
No filler about the checklist's identity is added to the pointer

evals.prompt: My skill's description says: "This skill helps with working on database migrations in various situations, including when migrating, when running migrations, when migration changes are needed, and other migration things." It almost never fires when it should. Rewrite it.
evals.expected_output: A description that carries distinct branches in a short, front-loaded pointer.
expectations: The write-for-agents skill is invoked because the user is editing a skill
SKILL-MECHANICS.md is read, since the document being edited is a skill
Synonymous triggers (migrating, running migrations, migration things) are collapsed into one branch each, keeping only genuinely distinct cases
The rewritten description is shorter than the original and opens with the leading word (migration) or the work it covers
The rewrite is model-facing and does not add disable-model-invocation or similar flags

evals.prompt: Use write-for-agents to review and tighten evals/files/AGENTS.md. It is the steering file for our Cobblestone invoicing service. Edit it in place and tell me what you changed and why.
evals.expected_output: A shorter AGENTS.md that keeps the unwritten convention and the deploy gotcha, and drops no-ops, restated commands, duplicates, and stale lines.
expectations: The two be-careful lines ('be thorough and careful', 'Always be careful and write high quality code') and the duplicate 'Always write high quality code' are removed as whole sentences, as no-ops and duplication
The Commands section that restates package.json scripts is removed or reduced, since the environment is the source of truth
The integer-cents rule is kept, with its reason (the payment provider rejects decimals, rounding bugs shipped twice), because no config confesses it
The reference to docs/legacy-importer.md is removed because the file no longer exists (stale)
'Never use var. Never use any. Never leave console.log statements in.' is rewritten as positive instructions (state the target behavior) or removed if the linter already enforces it
The five-step deploy runbook is moved behind a pointer to a separate file, or the rollback gotcha is kept while generic steps are cut, rather than left inline in an always-loaded file
The summary reports each change by its failure mode (no-op, duplication, cache, stale material, sprawl) and does not claim functionality was preserved without checking what was kept
The result is shorter than the input
No meaning is stated twice in the result

evals.prompt: Use write-for-agents on evals/files/draft-steps.md. I'm worried the agent will rush through it and skip testing.
evals.expected_output: Each step ends on a checkable completion criterion; the bound is sharpened before any split is considered.
expectations: Each of the four steps ends on a stated completion criterion that distinguishes done from not done
The vague 'Understand the codebase' bound is sharpened first (for example, every import style in the target file accounted for), not left as 'understanding reached'
The 'Test it' step names what is run and what a pass means, in demanding terms rather than 'produce a test report'
Hiding later steps by splitting the sequence is proposed only as a second move if the sharpened bound still fails, and the agent notes it only works across a real context boundary
SKILL-MECHANICS.md is read because the document is a skill

evals.prompt: Use write-for-agents. My SKILL.md is 600 lines and agents seem to lose track in the middle. About 150 lines apply to every run. Another 150 apply only when the tracker is GitHub, 150 only for GitLab, and 150 only for Jira. How should I restructure it? Show the new layout and the pointer lines, no need to write all 600 lines.
evals.expected_output: A restructure that inlines what every branch needs and discloses each tracker branch behind its own pointer.
expectations: The advice names the failure as sprawl and applies progressive disclosure: the shared 150 lines stay in SKILL.md
Each tracker's 150 lines moves to its own sibling file behind a context pointer
Each pointer names the file and states the one condition that triggers reading it, with the trigger word first
The three tracker files are not merged into one pointer to a combined file, since each run needs only one branch
The plan keeps in-file steps in order and does not hide material the agent needs on every run

evals.prompt: Write the SKILL.md for a new skill called post-release-notes that publishes our release notes to the team's chat channel after I approve the text. It must be safe to have in a skill list that other skills can call.
evals.expected_output: A new skill whose description is wordable around an explicit request, with the approval gate kept in the body.
expectations: The write-for-agents skill is invoked and SKILL-MECHANICS.md is read because the document is a skill
The frontmatter omits disable-model-invocation and carries a model-facing description
The description words the trigger around the user's explicit request to publish, because the skill has outward effects
The body keeps an approval step that shows the exact text and destination before posting, so a caller reaching the skill still stops there
Each step ends in a stated completion criterion, and the approval step's criterion is an explicit user approval

evals.prompt: Write a README for my open-source parsing library. It should explain what it does, how to install it, and show two usage examples for developers who find it on GitHub.
evals.expected_output: A README is human-facing documentation; the document skill handles it, not agent-instruction writing.
expectations: The write-for-agents skill is not invoked
The document skill, which covers READMEs and API references, is the one that shapes the work

evals.prompt: Here's a blog post draft that's full of filler and 'in order to' phrases. Tighten the wording so it reads like a person wrote it: "In order to make the most of the platform, it is important to note that users should leverage the dashboard."
evals.expected_output: Editing prose of a post for readers is the unslop skill's job.
expectations: The write-for-agents skill is not invoked
The unslop skill handles the edit, producing shorter plain text such as 'To get the most from the platform, use the dashboard'
